messages.subject: Thermal exchange equations for Multi-part animal geometries
messages.subject_clean: Thermal exchange equations for Multi-part animal geometries
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,

NicheMapR constructs animals as joined cylinders, ellipsoids, and other geometric shapes. I am writing to kindly request your assistance in providing me with references or resources that elucidate how thermodynamic equations can be applied when assembling animals using these geometric shapes. Despite my efforts to review the papers cited on the NicheMapR website and GitHub, I have been unable to locate the specific information I require.

An illustrated example, if possible, would certainly help me understand how to construct an animal from scratch using various shapes.

In addition, when one wants to add 2 or 3 layers (e.g. skin, fat, core) on the model animal, things can get complicated with the geometries, so if your answer can cover this too I will be very grateful.

Thanks in advance!

Alexandros

messages.subject: Re: Thermal exchange equations for Multi-part animal geometries
messages.subject_clean: Thermal exchange equations for Multi-part animal geometries
messages.body_plain:
Hi Alexandros,

This took me a little while to get to. I've been doing this kind of calculation specifically for simulating humans as a multi-part organism, which I haven't yet published. At some point when I have time I'll create some generic functions for this but, in the meantime, here is an example of what the calculation looks like to get you started.

If we to consider, for example, the organism as made up of cylinders, we can get the surface areas of these cylinders but not all this area is involved in exchange with the environment because there is a part of each cylinder that is joined to the rest of the body. We can simply assume that these joined bits are exchanging heat by conduction to a 'substrate' that is at body temperature. Thus we can achieve this by passing the correct shape factors for each body part (shape_b, to go from mass and density to shape) and also the correct p_cond values to make sure that not all of the object is exchanging with the environment.

The code below sets this up. It probably is wise to give it a careful check! Let me know if you spot any issues.

get_shapes <- function(AMASSs){
# Function to get the shape correction factors from a vector of masses of
# defined shapes and surface areas for an animal with a head, arms and legs.
# This function uses a root finding method to find the value of the shape
# correction factor that produces a shape with the stated surface area. However,
# the stated surface area should not include where it joins the rest
# of the body, and these joins are consider as exchanging heat by conduction
# to a surface at core body temperature. So, from the preliminary shape
# adjustment factors a vector of fractional conduction areas (i.e., the joins)
# is determined for each shape and the shape factor adjusted to account
# for this in the final estimate of 'shape_b' for each shape. The shape_b
# estimates and conduction fractions per shape are returned.
  # shape of each body part
  SHAPE_Bs <- AMASSs * 0
  PCONDs <- rep(0, length(AMASSs))
  for(i in 1:length(AMASSs)){
    # find SHAPE_B that matches body part surface area
    SHAPE_Bs[i] <- uniroot(function(xx) TOTSA * SAFRACs[i] - GEOM_ENDO(AMASSs[i], ANDENS, FATPCT, SHAPEs[i], 0, SUBQFAT, xx, xx, (DHAIRD + DHAIRV) / 2, (RHODs[i] + RHOVs[i]) / 2, PCONDs[i], 0, 0, 0)[8], lower = 1.1, upper = 500, tol = 0.0001)$root / 10
  }
  GEOM.lab <- c("VOL", "D", "MASFAT", "VOLFAT", "ALENTH", "AWIDTH",
                "AHEIT", "ATOT", "ASIL", "ASILN", "ASILP", "GMASS", "AREASKIN",
                "FLSHVL", "FATTHK", "ASEMAJ", "BSEMIN", "CSEMIN", "CONVSK",
                "CONVAR", "R1", "R2")
  geom.trunk <- as.data.frame(GEOM_ENDO(AMASSs[2], ANDENS, FATPCT, SHAPEs[2], 0, SUBQFAT, SHAPE_Bs[2], SHAPE_Bs[2], (DHAIRD + DHAIRV) / 2, (RHODs[2] + RHOVs[2]) / 2, PCONDs[2], 0, 0, 0))
  geom.arm <- as.data.frame(GEOM_ENDO(AMASSs[3], ANDENS, FATPCT, SHAPEs[3], 0, SUBQFAT, SHAPE_Bs[3], SHAPE_Bs[3], (DHAIRD + DHAIRV) / 2, (RHODs[3] + RHOVs[3]) / 2, PCONDs[3], 0, 0, 0))
  geom.leg <- as.data.frame(GEOM_ENDO(AMASSs[4], ANDENS, FATPCT, SHAPEs[4], 0, SUBQFAT, SHAPE_Bs[4], SHAPE_Bs[4], (DHAIRD + DHAIRV) / 2, (RHODs[4] + RHOVs[4]) / 2, PCONDs[4], 0, 0, 0))
  colnames(geom.trunk) <- GEOM.lab
  colnames(geom.arm) <- GEOM.lab
  colnames(geom.leg) <- GEOM.lab
  pcond.arm <- pi * (geom.arm$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 / (2 * pi * (geom.arm$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 + pi * geom.arm$AWIDTH *geom.arm$ALENTH) # one end in contact
  pcond.leg <- pi * (geom.leg$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 / (2 * pi * (geom.leg$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 + pi * geom.leg$AWIDTH *geom.leg$ALENTH) # one end in contact
  pcond.head <- (pcond.arm + pcond.leg) / 2 # assuming it's in this proportion - may need adjustment
  pcond.trunk <- pi * (geom.trunk$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 / (2 * pi * (geom.trunk$AWIDTH / 2) ^ 2 + pi * geom.trunk$AWIDTH *geom.trunk$ALENTH) + pcond.head # two arms, two legs and a head attached
  PCONDs <- c(pcond.head, pcond.trunk, pcond.arm, pcond.leg) * 1  # fraction of body in contact with substrate (dec %)

  # adding conduction area to total area for working out SHAPE_Bs
  for(i in 1:length(AMASSs)){
    # find SHAPE_B that matches body part surface area
    SHAPE_Bs[i] <- uniroot(function(xx) TOTSA * SAFRACs[i] + TOTSA * SAFRACs[i] * PCONDs[i] - GEOM_ENDO(AMASSs[i], ANDENS, FATPCT, SHAPEs[i], 0, SUBQFAT, xx, xx, (DHAIRD + DHAIRV) / 2, (RHODs[i] + RHOVs[i]) / 2, PCONDs[i], 0, 0, 0)[8], lower = 1.1, upper = 500, tol = 0.0001)$root / 10
  }
  return(list(SHAPE_Bs = SHAPE_Bs, PCONDs = PCONDs))
}

# morphological traits
ANDENS <- 900 # kg/m3
SUBQFAT <- 1 # is subcutaneous fat present? (0 is no, 1 is yes)
FATPCT <- 25 # % body fat

SHAPEs <- c(1, 1, 1, 1) # cylinder (SHAPE = 1), sphere (SHAPE = 2) and ellipsoid (SHAPE = 4)
NPARTs <- c(1, 1, 2, 2) # 1 head, 1 torso, 2 arms, 2 legs
PVENs <- rep(0.5, 4) # maximum fraction of surface area that is ventral (dec %)

# part specific traits (head, trunk, arm, leg)
ZFURDs <- c(0.01, 0.003, 0, 0) # fur depth, dorsal (m)
ZFURVs <- c(0.01, 0.003, 0, 0) # fur depth, ventral (m)
RHODs <- rep(100000, 4) # hair density, dorsal (1/m2)
RHOVs <- rep(100000, 4) # hair density, ventral (1/m2)
DHAIRD <- 24E-06 # hair diameter, dorsal (m)
DHAIRV <- 24E-06 # hair diameter, ventral (m)
LHAIRD <- 10E-03 # hair length, dorsal (m)
LHAIRV <- 10E-03 # hair length, ventral (m)

# head cylinder
head.length <- 0.2
head.radius <- 0.2
head.area <- 2 * pi * head.radius * head.length
head.mass <- pi * head.radius ^ 2 * head.length * ANDENS

# trunk cylinder
trunk.length <- 0.8
trunk.radius <- 0.2
trunk.area <- 2 * pi * trunk.radius * trunk.length
trunk.mass <- pi * trunk.radius ^ 2 * trunk.length * ANDENS

# leg cylinder
leg.length <- 0.6
leg.radius <- 0.05
leg.area <- 2 * pi * leg.radius * leg.length
leg.mass <- pi * leg.radius ^ 2 * leg.length * ANDENS

# body mass props
body.mass.props <- as.matrix(c(head.mass, trunk.mass, leg.mass, leg.mass))
body.mass.props <- body.mass.props * 100 / sum(body.mass.props) / 100 # make it add up to 100% and turn to proportion
rownames(body.mass.props) <- c("head", "trunk", "arm", "leg")

# body surface area proportions
body.sa.props <- as.matrix(c(head.area, trunk.area, leg.area, leg.area))
rownames(body.sa.props) <- c("head", "trunk", "arm", "leg")

MASSFRACs <- body.mass.props
SAFRACs <- body.sa.props
TOTSA <- head.area + trunk.area + 4 * leg.area
TOTMASS <- 60 # total mass, kg
AMASSs <- MASSFRACs * TOTMASS

shapes <- get_shapes(AMASSs)
SHAPE_Bs <- shapes$SHAPE_Bs
SHAPE_Bs <- c(head.length / head.radius * 2, trunk.length / trunk.radius * 2, leg.length / leg.radius * 2, leg.length / leg.radius * 2)
PCONDs <- shapes$PCONDs
PCONDs_orig <- PCONDs
pcond.head <- PCONDs[1]
pcond.trunk <- PCONDs[2]
pcond.arm <- PCONDs[3]
pcond.leg <- PCONDs[4]

I'll try adding some more on this soon.

All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: simulating pond temperatures
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

I was wondering if this is still the best way to generate temperature profiles for water bodies, or if there is a way to run the container model without this workaround?

I am working on temperature responses of freshwater snails and this could be a great fit.

Best, Tiem

On Thursday, 18 March 2021 at 10:38:16 UTC+1 Michael Kearney wrote:
> Dear Dennis,
>
> You can use the ectotherm mode or the microclimate model to simulate pond depths and temperatures, but in a bit of a kludgy way.
>
> For the microclimate model approach, you simulate a clay-based substrate and put a multiplier on the rainfall to simulate a catchment. I've found this can predict pond depths extremely well for a shallow wetland - it captures both the rain input and the evaporation/seepage output mechanistically, but not the water temperature. To get a rough prediction of water temperature you can use the water-logged soil temperatures for different depths to get a rough estimate.
>
> Alternatively you can use the 'container' model of the ectotherm model, which simulates an open-topped container either sitting on the surface (like a paddling pool) or sunk into the ground, and you can optionally put a hole in it (constant drainage per day) and vary the fraction of the surface that evaporates (to simulate it being partly covered). This can be computationally more intensive but will give a more accurate estimate of what the water temperature would be at the centre of the pond.
>
> The main thing of course is to have some good data with which to test it. Down the track we may finish integrating the 'General Lake Model' with NicheMapR, which is a proper fully-physical model of a water body with stratification etc.
>
> I’ve put some example code together (using the micro_usa function) below to show you how to implement the two approaches. Note the ectotherm model simulation took about 25 mins for the 2 year simulation! And also note that you'll have to install the latest version of the ectotherm model for the code below to work because there was a bug in the error trapping preventing 'conthole' from being different to zero or one, but it's fixed as of today.
>
> All the best,
> Mike
>
> library(NicheMapR)
>
> # microclimate model approach
>
> # define textural soil properties for clay
> soilpro <- matrix(data = 0, nrow = 6, ncol = 5)
> colnames(soilpro) <- c('depth', 'blkdens', 'clay', 'silt', 'sand')
> soilpro[,1] <- c(2.5, 7.5, 22.5, 45, 80, 150)
> soilpro[,2] <- 1.4 # bulk density (Mg/m3)
> soilpro[,3] <- 90 # % clay
> soilpro[,4] <- 0.0 # % silt
> soilpro[,5] <- 10 # % sand
> DEP <- c(0, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45, 90, 200) # Soil nodes (cm)
>
> # get hydraulic properties for given soil
> soil.hydro <- pedotransfer(soilpro = as.data.frame(soilpro), DEP = DEP)
> PE <- soil.hydro$PE
> BB <- soil.hydro$BB
> BD <- soil.hydro$BD
> KS <- soil.hydro$KS
> BulkDensity <- BD[seq(1, 19, 2)]
>
> rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
> maxpool <- 500 # maximium pooling depth (mm), i.e. wetland depth
> LAI <- 0 # leaf area index (zero so no transpiration)
> cap <- 0 # do not simulate the organic cap layer
> soilgrids <- 0 # don't use SoilGrids soil database for thermal properties
>
> micro <- micro_usa(PE = PE, BB = BB, BD = BD, KS = KS, rainmult = rainmult, maxpool = maxpool, LAI = LAI, cap = cap, soilgrids = soilgrids)
> metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
> soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)
> wetlandDepths<-as.data.frame(cbind(dates,as.data.frame(metout$POOLDEP)))
> colnames(wetlandDepths) <- c('dates', 'pond depth')
>
> # get closest soil depths for each wetland depth
> depth <- apply(as.matrix(wetlandDepths$depth / 10), 1, function(x) which.min(abs(x - DEP)))
> depth <- depth - 2 # actually choose 2 nodes shallower to better approximate amplitude
> depth[depth <= 0] <- 1 # step above produces some values below one - correct this
>
> # now get the soil temperatures for the corresponding wetland depths
> wetlandTemps <- as.data.frame(as.numeric(soil[cbind(seq_along(depth + 3), depth + 3)]))
> wetlandTemps <- cbind(dates, wetlandTemps) # append dates
> colnames(wetlandTemps) <- c('dates', 'pond temperature')
>
> par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
> plot(wetlandDepths, type = 'l', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'microclimate model prediction')
> plot(wetlandTemps, type = 'l', ylim = c(-20, 50))
>
> # ectotherm model approach
>
> # container model parameters
> container <- 1 # Run the water body/container model? (aquatic start of life cycle, e.g. frog or mosquito)
> conth <- 500 # Cylindrical container/pond height (mm)
> contw <- 10000 # Cylindrical container/pond diameter (mm)
> contype <- 1 # Is 'container' sitting on the surface, like a bucket (0) or sunk into the ground like a pond (1)
> rainmult <- 4.5 # Rainfall multiplier to reflect catchment (1 will result in unadjusted rainfall)
> continit <- 0 # Initial container water level (cm)
> conthole <- 10 # Daily (or hourly if rainhr vector filled) loss of height (mm) due to 'hole' in container (e.g. infiltration to soil, drawdown from water tank)
> contonly <- 1 # Just run the container model and quit?
> contwet <- 100 # % of container surface acting as a free water exchanger
>
> # run the ectotherm model (this is quite slow! ~ 25 mins)
> ecto <- ectotherm(container = container, conth = conth, contw = contw, contype = contype,
>                   rainmult = rainmult, continit = continit, conthole = conthole,
>                   contonly = contonly, contwet = contwet)
> environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
> plot(micro$dates, environ$CONDEP, type = 'l', ylab = 'container depth', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(0, 500), main = 'ectotherm model prediction')
> plot(micro$dates, environ$TC, type = 'l', ylab = 'water temperature', xlab = 'date', ylim = c(-20, 50))
>
>
> On Thursday, March 18, 2021 at 6:44:51 PM UTC+11 dennis....@googlemail.com wrote:
> > Dear Mike,
> >
> > in your Ecography paper introducing the NicheMapR R package you announce another study introducing the ectotherm model to simulate pond conditons
> >
> > "The ectotherm model also has scope to estimate transient heat budgets, and thus stored heat, QS, but without thermoregulatory behaviour. This functionality can also be used to estimate water temperatures in a ‘bucket model’ simulation of a container filling with rainwater which can be used to simulate ponds and other waterbodies under certain assumptions. These aspects of the model will be described elsewhere."
> >
> > Having temperature profiles for pond strata would be awsome and very helpful for my projects. Is there already a descrption how to simulate this kind of pond microclimates?
> >
> > Thank you so much in advance,
> > best wishes
> > Dennis
